semantic_correction.stem: A breastfeeding client is returning to work and wants to maintain milk production while separated from the infant. Which teaching is most appropriate?

options.A: Pump about as often as the baby usually drinks breast milk while they are apart.
options.B: Wait until the breasts feel very full before pumping, even when this creates long gaps between sessions.
options.C: Reduce daytime milk removal after returning to work so the body gradually learns to store more milk.
options.D: Stop pumping during the workday and rely on breastfeeding only before and after work to maintain supply.

semantic_correction.rationale: CDC guidance updated February 24, 2026 advises people who are away from their baby or exclusively pumping to pump about as often as the baby is drinking breast milk. CDC explains that this regular milk removal helps signal the body to keep making approximately the amount of milk the baby needs; if pumping enough milk is difficult, an additional pumping session may help increase supply. Therefore option A best supports continued milk production during work-related separation.
semantic_correction.educational_objective: Teach that pumping about as often as the infant normally drinks breast milk during separation supports continued milk production.
semantic_correction.source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
semantic_correction.source_document_title: Pumping Breast Milk; Breastfeeding and Returning to Your Workplace

semantic_correction.source_locator: Pumping Breast Milk — How often to pump: when away from baby or exclusively pumping, try to pump as often as the baby is drinking breast milk; this helps the body keep making the amount the baby needs. How much to pump: pumping at the baby's usual feeding frequency supports supply and an extra session may help if output is insufficient. Returning to Your Workplace — plan how often pumping or expression will be needed while apart

semantic_correction.correction_summary_append: RULE1 cleanup: removed the absolute-word distractor, narrowed the item to the directly tested milk-supply concept, and anchored the correct response to CDC's February 2026 pumping-frequency guidance.

audit_findings_append.source_locator: Pumping Breast Milk — How often to pump; Returning to Your Workplace

audit_findings_append.finding: The revised item directly tests frequency of milk expression during separation without adding unnecessary legal or workplace-coverage complexity to the answer set.

option_audit.A: Correct. It directly matches CDC guidance for maintaining milk production during separation.
option_audit.B: Incorrect. Long gaps in milk removal do not reflect the CDC recommendation to pump at the baby's usual feeding frequency.
option_audit.C: Incorrect. Reducing milk removal is inconsistent with the supply-supporting principle of regular expression.
option_audit.D: Incorrect. Eliminating workday pumping can create prolonged intervals inconsistent with the stated goal of maintaining supply.

ambiguity_check: No second defensible answer. A alone directly applies the CDC-recommended pumping frequency to the work-separation scenario.
cueing_check: All four options are pumping-frequency strategies of comparable length and specificity; no absolute-word or unique-length cue identifies A.
